explanations.answer: Without words by how their wives live
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Peter says even husbands who refuse to believe the word "will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives" (1 Peter 3:1). No speech needed. Their lives do the talking, and I think that takes a lot of quiet strength.

explanations.answer: By hearing their wives preach to them
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Peter goes the other way. He says husbands are won over "without words" (1 Peter 3:1). So the sermon isn't a speech at all. It's how the wives live, and I think that's a louder sermon than most.

explanations.answer: By a visit from the church elders
explanations.explanation: No elders knocking on the door in this verse, friend. Peter says the husbands are won over "without words by the behavior of their wives" (1 Peter 3:1). The wives' own lives are what do the work. Nobody has to bring a committee.

explanations.answer: The inner disposition of the heart
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Peter says beauty comes "from the inner disposition of your heart" (1 Peter 3:4). He's pointing past braids, gold and fine clothes to the inside. Nobody can wrap that up in a box, and nobody can polish it either.

explanations.answer: The good reputation of the family
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, friend, but Peter doesn't mention family reputation here. He says beauty comes "from the inner disposition of your heart" (1 Peter 3:4). It's about what's inside a person, not what the neighbors say about the family.

explanations.answer: The steady labor of the hands
explanations.explanation: Hard work is a fine thing, and my mustache has put in plenty of it. But Peter doesn't point to the hands here. He says beauty comes "from the inner disposition of your heart" (1 Peter 3:4). It's an inside job.

True, baker! Peter calls it "the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (1 Peter 3:4). Hair gets messy and clothes wear out. I know a thing or two about edges getting worn down, friend. This kind of beauty doesn't fade.

Peter actually says the opposite, friend. He calls it "the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God's sight" (1 Peter 3:4). Unfading means it doesn't wear out. I could have used some of that back in my drawer days.

That's right, baker. Peter says the holy women of the past "put their hope in God" (1 Peter 3:5). Their hope wasn't in how they looked or who they knew. It was in Him, and that's the best place to park it.

Nice guess, friend, but angels aren't in this verse. Peter says those holy women "put their hope in God" (1 Peter 3:5). Angels are great, and one of them once called me out of a drawer, but the hope goes to God Himself.
No kings in this verse, friend. Peter says the holy women of the past "put their hope in God" (1 Peter 3:5). Crowns come and go, but God is the One worth hoping in.

You got it, baker. Peter says they are Sarah's children "if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear" (1 Peter 3:6). Doing right and refusing fear go together in that line. Fear can be loud, but it doesn't have to win.

Anger shows up later in this passage, friend, but not in this line. Peter says they are Sarah's children "if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear" (1 Peter 3:6). The thing to refuse here is fear.
Peter doesn't say anything about leaving home here, friend. He says they are Sarah's children "if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear" (1 Peter 3:6). Fear is the thing to say no to.

explanations.answer: Fellow heirs of the gift of life
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Peter says to honor wives "as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life" (1 Peter 3:7). Fellow heirs means they share in it together. Nobody is standing on a higher shelf in that kitchen.

Good try, friend, but Peter doesn't use that title. He says to honor wives "as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life" (1 Peter 3:7). Fellow heirs means husband and wife receive that gift together.

explanations.answer: Guests to be served with care
explanations.explanation: Sounds nice, friend, but that's not what Peter says. Husbands are to honor their wives "as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life" (1 Peter 3:7). Guests are visitors. Heirs share the same inheritance.

Peter says the opposite, friend. He tells husbands to treat their wives with consideration and honor "so that your prayers will not be hindered" (1 Peter 3:7). So how a husband treats his wife is tied to his prayers. That's one to remember.

False is right, baker. Peter says husbands should treat their wives well "so that your prayers will not be hindered" (1 Peter 3:7). The two are connected. Home life and prayer life aren't in separate rooms.

Not quite, friend. Peter says to all of them, "be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble" (1 Peter 3:8). Those are things you show to one another, not things you bottle up inside.

False is right, baker. Peter tells them all to "be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble" (1 Peter 3:8). Nothing about keeping it all inside. Those are meant to be shown to each other.

That's the one, baker! Peter says not to repay evil with evil or insult with insult, "but with blessing" (1 Peter 3:9). Somebody throws a jab and you hand back a blessing. Now THAT will surprise them.
Walking away sounds smart, friend, but that's not the word. Peter says to repay evil and insult "but with blessing" (1 Peter 3:9). He wants a blessing sent back, not just space.
A warning might feel fair in the moment, friend, but Peter picks a different word. He says to repay evil and insult "but with blessing" (1 Peter 3:9). Blessing is the answer he gives.

Right on, baker. The quote says whoever would love life "must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech" (1 Peter 3:10). Words get a lot of attention in this passage. A little muscle, a big deal.
You got it, friend. The quote says "he must seek peace and pursue it" (1 Peter 3:11). Seek it AND pursue it. Peter doesn't tell them to sit around waiting for peace to show up.
Hands are useful, and mine are made of mustache, but that's not the word. The quote says to "keep his tongue from evil" (1 Peter 3:10). The tongue is the one that goes in the first blank.
No money talk in this quote, friend. It says "keep his tongue from evil" (1 Peter 3:10) and "seek peace and pursue it" (1 Peter 3:11). Tongue and peace are the words that fit the blanks.
Eyes do show up in the next verse, but about the Lord, not about the person. This quote says to "keep his tongue from evil" (1 Peter 3:10). The tongue is what fits the first blank.
That's right, baker. The quote says "the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer" (1 Peter 3:12). He sees them and He hears them. That's a good thing to know.

Wisdom is a good thing, friend, but that's not the word here. The quote says "His ears are inclined to their prayer," and the "their" is the righteous (1 Peter 3:12). So the righteous are the ones named.

No wallet check at the door, friend. The quote says "the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer" (1 Peter 3:12). The righteous are the ones named, not the wealthy.
